message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
Here's everything for tomorrow.

**Van name ideas for the staff vote**

- **Dovetail**
- **Chester**, as in chest of drawers
- **Polly**, for French polish
- **Veneer-a**
- **The Wardrobe**, because things go in and come out somewhere else entirely
- **Sandy**

**Delivery order: Depot → B → A → C → Depot**

That's the only order that works. Going to A first doesn't work: arriving at 09:00, unloading until 09:15 and then driving 25 minutes gets to B at 09:40, after it opens. C can't be done until 11:00, so it has to be last.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B**, unload |
| 09:05 | Leave B, done before the 09:30 opening ✅ |
| 09:30 | Arrive at **A**, unload, inside the 09:00–10:00 window ✅ |
| 09:45 | Finish at A |
| 09:45–10:15 | **30-minute break** (near A) |
| 10:15 | Leave A |
| 10:55 | Arrive at **C**, wait 5 minutes |
| 11:00 | Unload at C, the earliest it will accept ✅ |
| 11:15 | Leave C |
| 12:00 | **Back at depot** ✅ |

**One warning: the end of the day has zero slack.** C can't start before 11:00, unloading takes 15 minutes and the drive back is 45, so 12:00 is the earliest possible return. If C keeps him waiting even a few minutes, or traffic is bad, he'll be late. Two options:
- Ask C whether they can take the delivery at 10:45 or 10:50.
- Tell the depot in advance that a return around 12:15 is possible.

The morning has some room. He could leave as late as about 08:45 and still make B and A in time, but 08:30 gives him a buffer.

**Friendlier "on the way" text**

> Hi [Name], it's [driver] from [Business]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

**Three things to check on the furniture before handing it over**

1. **Condition:** no new scratches, dents or marks from transit. Compare against the restorer's finish photos if you have them.
2. **Working parts:** drawers slide, doors open and close properly, and all handles, knobs, keys and shelves are present.
3. **Placement and stability:** it's in the right room and position, sits level without rocking, and the customer is happy with it before signing.

**Paper or emailed delivery note?**

**Emailed**, with the customer signing on the driver's phone or tablet. It's harder to lose, it's searchable if there's a dispute later, and you can attach photos of the item as delivered. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who'd rather have one or can't receive email.

**Proof of delivery, for the part-timer**

> Proof of delivery is the record, usually a customer signature plus the date, time and sometimes a photo, showing that the item was delivered to the right person in good condition.

**Evening-before text (under 160 characters)**

> Hi [Name], [Business] here! Your furniture delivery is due tomorrow between [9-10am]. Please reply if that time doesn't suit. Thanks!

That's about 133 characters with the placeholders as written. It leaves room for most names, but keep the business name short. Two tips to make sure it actually sends as one message:
- Avoid emojis.
- Use a straight apostrophe (') in "doesn't" rather than a curly one (’). Special characters can switch the whole text to a different encoding with a 70-character limit per message, which would split it into three.
